name: Preference
plain_language: A way to say which outcome a person would rather have.
why_it_exists: Choices need an internal ordering; without one, better and worse have no operational meaning.
formal_object: A preference relation ranks outcomes, often represented by a utility function u(x).
useful_equation: x preferred to y means u(x) > u(y).
symbol_explanation: x and y are possible outcomes; u assigns each outcome a number; the larger number records the option the person ranks higher.
misuse_failure: Treating utility as literal happiness can mislead; in game theory it is a ranking device for choices.
everyday_setup: Imagine choosing between two concrete outcomes: more money with more risk, less money with less risk, agreement now, or a chance of a better agreement later. Preference is the ordered list hiding behind that choice.
course_appearances: Preferences appear first in the opening choice lecture, then reappear whenever payoffs, utilities, outside options, bidder values, or expected utilities are used as inputs to strategic reasoning.
plain_language_principle: Preference is the course’s way of saying that a person can compare outcomes before any strategic machinery starts. The primitive matters because a game cannot explain choice unless there is some stable sense in which one outcome is better for that player than another.
why_it_matters: It makes later payoff comparisons meaningful without forcing the course to measure inner happiness directly. The math only needs the ranking behavior that is relevant for choice.
misuse_warning: The common misuse is treating the utility representation as a literal psychological ruler. In this course, different numerical representations can describe the same ordering unless uncertainty or expected utility requires stronger comparisons.
first_principles_pressure: The pressure is that choice has to happen before strategy can be analyzed. If the model cannot say which outcome a player would rather have, then later words like payoff, incentive, or deviation have no anchor. Preference is the smallest object that turns desire into an inspectable ordering.
worked_micro_case: Suppose a bidder would rather win an item at a low price than win it at a high price, and would rather lose than win while paying above value. Those rankings are the primitive. The auction model can later attach numbers, but the ordering is what tells the model what counts as better.
transfer_test: When meeting a new model, ask what outcomes the actor is being asked to rank. If the model jumps straight to a payoff number, translate it back into the ranking it is supposed to preserve. If that ranking is unclear or unstable, the rest of the strategic analysis is already fragile.

name: Payoff Mapping
plain_language: A table that says what each person gets from each combination of choices.
why_it_exists: In strategic settings, my result depends on what others do too.
formal_object: A payoff function u_i(a_i, a_-i) maps everyone's actions to player i's payoff.
symbol_explanation: i is one player; a_i is that player's action; a_-i means everyone else's actions; u_i is the payoff assigned to the whole action profile.
misuse_failure: A payoff table is not the world itself; it is a simplified representation whose assumptions drive the result.
everyday_setup: A firm’s profit depends on its own price and a rival’s price; a bargainer’s payoff depends on both the offer and the response; an auction payoff depends on the bid, rivals’ bids, value, and payment rule.
course_appearances: Payoff mapping appears in strategic-form games, extensive-form games, bargaining, ad auctions, and any lecture that asks whether a deviation changes a player’s payoff.
plain_language_principle: Payoff mapping says that one person’s result is produced by the whole situation, not by that person’s action alone. A game table or tree is a compact machine that turns everyone’s choices into each player’s consequence.
why_it_matters: It prevents the analyst from evaluating actions as isolated moves. Once the payoff map is written down, best responses, dominance, equilibrium, and mechanism design have something precise to inspect.
misuse_warning: A payoff map can smuggle in the conclusion if the modeler omits costs, outside options, information, or future consequences. The table is only as honest as the situation it represents.
first_principles_pressure: The pressure is interaction. In ordinary decision-making, an action can be judged by its own consequence. In a game, the consequence is produced by several choices at once, so the model needs a map from the whole situation to each person's payoff.
worked_micro_case: If two firms both choose prices, one firm's profit from a high price depends on whether the rival also stays high or undercuts. The same action can be profitable in one cell and damaging in another. The payoff map keeps those cell-by-cell consequences visible.
transfer_test: When reading a strategic model, locate the sentence or table that says how outcomes are produced from everyone’s actions. Then ask what has been omitted: timing, information, outside options, future punishments, or costs. Missing pieces in the payoff map become hidden assumptions in every later result.

name: Best Response
plain_language: The choice that works best given what someone believes others will do.
why_it_exists: No strategy is good in isolation; it is good against some expectation about others.
formal_object: BR_i(a_-i) is the set of actions for player i that maximize u_i given others' actions.
symbol_explanation: argmax means choose the action a that makes player i's payoff as large as possible when others choose a_-i.
misuse_failure: Calling something a best response without naming the belief or opponent action hides the key assumption.
everyday_setup: If a rival sets a high price, one response may be best; if the rival cuts price, another response may be best. The action is not universally good; it is good against a specified situation.
course_appearances: Best response appears in rationalizability, Nash equilibrium, mixed strategies, minimax reasoning, Bayesian Nash equilibrium, and the deviation checks behind dynamic concepts.
plain_language_principle: Best response is the one-player optimization step inside game theory, but in everyday words it means: given what I think the others are doing, what should I do?
why_it_matters: It is the local test behind nearly every solution concept. Equilibrium is built by making many best-response checks hold at the same time.
misuse_warning: The misuse is naming a best response without naming the belief, opponent action, or information condition. That hides the actual assumption doing the work.
first_principles_pressure: The pressure is conditional choice. A move is not good in empty space; it is good after the player forms an expectation about the environment. Best response exists because the model must separate the action chosen from the condition under which it is chosen.
worked_micro_case: A store may cut price if the rival keeps price high, but keep price high if both firms are avoiding a price war. Neither action is simply best. Each is best against a different rival behavior, which is why the condition belongs inside the primitive.
transfer_test: Whenever a paper says an action is optimal, ask: optimal against what? Name the rival action, belief, type, or history being held fixed. If the condition changes and the action no longer wins, the result is a conditional best response, not a universal recommendation. A good transfer reading should also identify the choice set being searched; if some actions are omitted, the best-response claim is only relative to that restricted menu.

name: Mutual Consistency
plain_language: A situation where each person's plan makes sense given everyone else's plan.
why_it_exists: A prediction of strategic behavior must survive every player asking whether they personally want to change.
formal_object: Equilibrium requires each strategy to be a best response to the others.
useful_equation: a_i in BR_i(a_-i) for every player i.
symbol_explanation: For each player i, their chosen action a_i must belong to the set of best responses against the other players' actions.
misuse_failure: Equilibrium does not mean fair, efficient, or morally good; it means no one has a one-person reason to move.
everyday_setup: A traffic merge, price competition, or bidding situation can sound stable until one participant notices a better move. Mutual consistency means that no participant has that private reason to switch.
course_appearances: Mutual consistency appears in Nash equilibrium, mixed strategies, zero-sum games, subgame perfection, infinitely repeated games, folk theorem logic, and Bayesian Nash equilibrium.
plain_language_principle: Mutual consistency turns a collection of individual choices into a stable strategic prediction. Everyone’s plan has to make sense given everyone else’s plan.
why_it_matters: It is the reason equilibrium is a disciplined prediction rather than a story. The concept asks every player to audit the proposed outcome from their own incentive point of view.
misuse_warning: The misuse is reading equilibrium as good, fair, optimal for society, or morally desirable. It only says that unilateral deviation is not profitable under the modeled conditions.
first_principles_pressure: The pressure is circular dependence. My best move depends on yours, and yours depends on mine. A prediction has to close that loop without leaving one player wishing to revise after seeing the proposed outcome.
worked_micro_case: In a prisoner’s dilemma, mutual defection can be stable even though both players would prefer mutual cooperation. Each player audits the outcome from their own unilateral-deviation point of view. The bad social result survives because switching alone is worse under the modeled payoffs. This is why equilibrium can explain a stuck situation without praising it.
transfer_test: When a model claims equilibrium, perform the one-person switch test. Hold everyone else fixed and ask whether a player can improve. Then repeat for every player or type. If the answer is no, the profile has mutual consistency, even if it is inefficient or unattractive. If the model is dynamic or has hidden information, ask whether the same consistency test is being refined rather than abandoned.

name: Pruning
plain_language: Remove choices that are never worth taking, then reason with the smaller problem.
why_it_exists: Large strategic problems become easier when obviously bad options can be ruled out.
formal_object: Dominance compares one strategy against another across possible opponent choices.
useful_equation: s dominates t if u_i(s, a_-i) >= u_i(t, a_-i) for all a_-i, with strict inequality somewhere.
symbol_explanation: The inequality checks every possible action by others; dominance means one strategy is never worse and sometimes better.
misuse_failure: Pruning too aggressively can remove behavior that matters when beliefs, weak dominance, or timing are handled differently.
everyday_setup: If one route is slower no matter what traffic does, or one bid is worse no matter how rivals bid, a careful decision-maker should not keep treating it as live.
course_appearances: Pruning appears in dominance, iterated deletion, rationalizability, and as background for equilibrium reasoning because eliminated strategies cannot be serious best responses.
plain_language_principle: Pruning removes actions that cannot be justified before solving the whole game. It is the mathematical version of clearing away choices that are never worth taking.
why_it_matters: It reduces strategic clutter and teaches students that not every listed action deserves equal attention. It also shows how rationality assumptions can have observable consequences before equilibrium is imposed.
misuse_warning: The misuse is deleting too aggressively, especially with weak dominance or when beliefs matter. A deletion rule can change the remaining game, so the strength and order of the rule must be explicit.
first_principles_pressure: The pressure is attention. A game can list many actions, but some actions have no defensible reason to remain once payoffs are compared across contingencies. Pruning exists to remove choices that cannot survive even before a full prediction is built.
worked_micro_case: If a bidder strategy pays less than another strategy whether rivals bid low, medium, or high, keeping it alive only clutters the analysis. But if it wins under one rival case, deletion is no longer dominance; the analyst has moved into beliefs and best responses.
transfer_test: Before deleting an action, check every relevant opponent action or state. If the action loses everywhere, prune it. If it loses only under the scenario you expect, keep it and say what belief makes it unattractive. That distinction prevents a hunch from masquerading as proof. Also ask whether the deletion is strict or weak; weak deletion can change the remaining problem in ways that strict deletion usually does not.

name: Backward Recursion
plain_language: Solve the future first, then use that answer to decide what should happen earlier.
why_it_exists: In sequential games, later credible choices determine earlier incentives.
formal_object: Backward induction assigns optimal choices from terminal decision nodes back to the start.
symbol_explanation: V is continuation value; at each decision point the player chooses the next branch with the best continuation value.
misuse_failure: Backward induction assumes the game tree and payoffs are known and that later threats are credible.
everyday_setup: A threat to punish later is persuasive only if punishment will still be worth doing later. A buyer’s current offer depends on what both sides expect at the next bargaining step.
course_appearances: Backward recursion appears in extensive-form games, backward induction, subgame perfection, one-shot deviation, bargaining, finitely repeated games, and perfect Bayesian equilibrium.
plain_language_principle: Backward recursion says that later incentives determine earlier meaning. To understand a promise or threat now, solve what the player will want when the promised moment arrives.
why_it_matters: It gives sequential games their discipline. Instead of accepting announced plans, the course tests each continuation point and pulls those continuation values back to the start.
misuse_warning: The misuse is solving backward through a tree that leaves out information, uncertainty, or renegotiation. Backward logic is powerful only after the tree is an honest representation.
first_principles_pressure: The pressure is time. Earlier choices are shaped by what later selves or later players will actually want to do. Backward recursion exists because future incentives determine whether present threats, promises, and expectations are credible.
worked_micro_case: A seller may threaten to reject a low offer, but if rejection later leaves the seller with nothing, the threat may not survive the later decision node. Solving the end first tells the buyer whether the early threat changes the current bargaining problem. The same logic appears in finite repetition: the last round can decide what earlier rounds mean.
transfer_test: When a dynamic model includes a threat or promise, jump to the moment when it must be carried out. Ask what the player wants at that later point, ignoring earlier words. If the action is not best there, the model needs commitment, reputation, or a different tree. Then check whether the player observes enough history to know which later node they are actually in.

name: Discounting
plain_language: Future rewards count, but usually count less than rewards right now.
why_it_exists: Repeated relationships trade off today's temptation against tomorrow's consequences.
formal_object: A discount factor delta weights future payoffs in an intertemporal sum.
useful_equation: U = u_0 + delta u_1 + delta^2 u_2 + ...
symbol_explanation: u_t is payoff in period t; delta between 0 and 1 controls how strongly the future matters.
misuse_failure: A cooperation result can disappear when players are impatient or cannot punish future deviations.
everyday_setup: A firm may avoid undercutting today if it values future high prices enough. A bargainer may accept less now if waiting is costly or reject now if future surplus is valuable.
course_appearances: Discounting appears in bargaining, infinitely repeated games, folk theorem arguments, implicit cartels, and the repeated-game parts of cooperation.
plain_language_principle: Discounting is the course’s way to compare now with later. Future payoffs matter, but the discount factor says how much weight the future has relative to the present.
why_it_matters: It turns patience into a mathematical object. The survival of cooperation often depends on whether discounted future punishment is larger than immediate temptation.
misuse_warning: The misuse is treating future discipline as automatic. If players are impatient, cannot observe cheating, or know the game ends, the discounting inequality can fail.
first_principles_pressure: The pressure is distance in time. A payoff tomorrow can discipline behavior today only if the player cares enough about tomorrow. Discounting exists to turn patience into a number that can be compared against present temptation.
worked_micro_case: A cartel member can cut price today and gain immediately, but may trigger future price punishment. Cooperation survives only if the discounted future loss is larger than the one-time gain. The discount factor is what decides whether the future is heavy enough. If customers, rivals, or regulators make punishment slow or uncertain, the future becomes lighter in the current calculation.
transfer_test: For any repeated-game claim, write the immediate gain from deviation and the future loss from punishment. Then apply the discount factor. If the discounted future loss is too small, repetition is not doing the work the author says it is doing. Also check monitoring: a future punishment cannot discipline present behavior if players cannot tell that a deviation occurred. Finally, check whether the end date is known, because a known last period can strip future punishment of force.

name: Belief
plain_language: A probability story about what kind of situation or opponent you are facing.
why_it_exists: People often choose without knowing another person's type, value, cost, or information.
formal_object: A belief is a probability distribution over states, types, or histories.
useful_equation: E[u(a, theta)] = sum_theta p(theta) u(a, theta).
symbol_explanation: theta is the unknown type or state; p(theta) is its probability; expected utility averages payoffs across possibilities.
misuse_failure: If beliefs are not tied to information and incentives, the model can rationalize almost anything.
everyday_setup: A bidder estimates rivals’ values, a receiver estimates a sender’s type, and a player in a Bayesian game estimates which payoff situation they are facing.
course_appearances: Belief appears in expected utility, rationalizability, mixed strategies, Bayesian games, types and beliefs, Bayesian Nash equilibrium, auctions, PBE, signaling, and cheap talk.
plain_language_principle: Belief is a probability story about hidden facts. It lets a player choose while admitting that they do not know the opponent’s type, value, history, or information.
why_it_matters: It keeps uncertainty inside the model instead of pretending it away. Once beliefs are explicit, the course can ask whether actions are optimal under those beliefs and whether observations should update them.
misuse_warning: The misuse is using beliefs as arbitrary story glue. In dynamic games especially, beliefs must be tied to information, Bayes rule where possible, and the incentives that produced observed behavior.
first_principles_pressure: The pressure is hidden structure. Players often choose without knowing values, costs, types, histories, or motives. Belief exists because uncertainty has to be inside the model, not left as a vague background cloud.
worked_micro_case: A buyer sees a seller reject an offer. That rejection may suggest high cost, strong bargaining position, or strategic posturing. A belief assigns weights to these possibilities, and later equilibrium reasoning asks whether those weights are consistent with the behavior that produced the signal. The action is therefore both a move in the game and evidence about hidden structure.
transfer_test: When a model invokes belief, ask what the belief is over, where it came from, and how observations update it. If the belief can be changed freely to rescue any conclusion, it is no longer evidence discipline; it is decoration. In dynamic settings, also ask whether the observation is on the predicted path, because off-path beliefs need special care. A strong belief argument should say what evidence would move the belief and what evidence would leave it mostly unchanged.

name: Incentive Compatibility
plain_language: Design rules so people want to reveal or do what the rule needs them to reveal or do.
why_it_exists: People with private information may gain by misreporting it.
formal_object: Truthful behavior must give at least as much payoff as each profitable lie.
useful_equation: u_i(truth) >= u_i(report) for every alternative report.
symbol_explanation: The inequality says a person should not gain by replacing the truthful action with another report.
misuse_failure: A mechanism can look efficient on paper while failing because participants have incentives to shade bids or messages.
everyday_setup: A bidder may shade a bid, a sender may lie, a firm may cheat on a cartel, and a platform participant may respond to ranking rules. The question is whether the rules make the intended action the best move.
course_appearances: Incentive compatibility appears in implicit cartels, auctions, revenue equivalence, ad auctions, signaling, and cheap talk, with related logic in folk-theorem punishment constraints.
plain_language_principle: Incentive compatibility asks whether the rule makes desired behavior privately worthwhile. A mechanism cannot simply request honesty, cooperation, or truthful bidding; it must make those actions attractive.
why_it_matters: It is the design version of game theory. Instead of assuming people do what the designer wants, the course checks whether strategic self-interest leads there.
misuse_warning: The misuse is designing by intention rather than incentives. If misreporting, deviation, or manipulation pays more, the mechanism fails no matter how elegant the rule looks.
first_principles_pressure: The pressure is private advantage. A rule may want people to reveal information, keep cooperating, bid honestly, or send useful messages, but participants compare the requested behavior against profitable alternatives. Incentive compatibility exists because a rule must survive self-interest.
worked_micro_case: In an auction, a platform may want bidders to reveal values, but a bidder may gain by shading the bid. The mechanism has to make the desired report or action at least as good as the manipulation. Otherwise the rule describes a wish, not a strategic outcome. The same check applies to cartel punishment, cheap talk, and signaling: desired behavior must be privately worth choosing.
transfer_test: When reading a mechanism, identify the intended behavior and then list the tempting lies, deviations, or manipulations. Compare payoffs for each. If any alternative pays more, the design is not incentive compatible under the stated assumptions. Then ask whether the information needed to enforce the rule is actually observed by the participants or platform.

name: Knowledge Recursion
plain_language: Not only knowing a fact, but knowing that others know it, and so on.
why_it_exists: Coordinated strategic behavior often depends on shared awareness, not private awareness alone.
formal_object: Common knowledge means everyone knows, everyone knows everyone knows, and the chain continues.
symbol_explanation: E is the event; K means known by the players; repeated K's represent higher-order knowledge.
misuse_failure: Treating public facts as common knowledge can be wrong if people are unsure what others observed.
everyday_setup: A public announcement can coordinate people because each person knows that everyone else heard it. A private message may give the same fact to one person without creating that shared confidence.
course_appearances: Knowledge recursion appears most directly in common knowledge, and indirectly in iterated deletion, rationalizability, equilibrium selection, and communication because players reason about others’ reasoning.
plain_language_principle: Knowledge recursion captures the difference between a fact being true, people knowing it, and people knowing that others know it. Coordination often needs the higher levels, not just the first one.
why_it_matters: It explains why publicness can be strategically powerful. Some outcomes require not only information but shared awareness that the information is shared.
misuse_warning: The misuse is treating widespread knowledge as common knowledge. If players are unsure whether others saw the same fact, the recursive chain can break and coordination may fail.
first_principles_pressure: The pressure is coordinated confidence. Sometimes knowing a fact is not enough; a player also needs confidence that others know it, and confidence that others know that everyone knows it. Knowledge recursion exists because coordination can depend on those higher layers.
worked_micro_case: Two investors may both receive similar private warnings, but each may wonder whether the other received them too. A public announcement can change behavior even if it adds little new factual content, because it creates shared awareness that the warning is shared. The informational payload is not only the fact; it is the publicness of the fact.
transfer_test: When a coordination model uses information, ask whether the fact is private, mutual, public, or common knowledge. If action requires confidence about others' confidence, a private signal may be too weak even when every player individually knows the same fact. Then ask whether the model needs one level of knowledge or an unbounded recursive chain. In a new paper, look for public announcements, shared protocols, or visible histories; those are often attempts to create the recursive confidence the result needs.
